title: How To Smash The Memory Wall Plaguing High Performance Systems
gist: A guest architect proposes replacing linear physical memory addressing inside the CPU with a hardwired Z-Order (Morton) layout, using AMD's 128-core 'Turin' Epyc 9005 with 16 CCXs as the reference topology, and pairs it with distributed 4-bit Counting Bloom filters in the NoC routers and Tropf-Hertzog BIGMIN/LITMAX range filters at L2 and L3. The claimed payoff is the elimination of broadcast snoop traffic, 4 KB spatial-hypercube cache fills, SmartNIC/RDMA coherence checks without core stalls, ~250 ns recovered on CXL tail latency, and large SRAM tag-array power savings — explicitly for a specialized HPC/AI/analytics part, not a general-purpose CPU. It is a theoretical design proposal from a practitioner, not a shipping product.

insights.claim: Modern 128-core server CPUs routinely fall short of peak theoretical performance on analytical workloads because cores sit idle waiting on RAM transfers, not because of a shortage of compute throughput.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Compute-per-dollar benchmarks overstate delivered value in data analytics; memory-hierarchy differentiation, not core count, is where the next round of server-CPU pricing power sits.
insights.quote: I repeatedly watch today’s most advanced server processors fall short of their peak theoretical performance. A primary culprit? Cores sitting idle, waiting for data transfers from RAM.
insights.locator: In my day-to-day work, I process massive

insights.claim: The core architectural failure is a 40-year-old mental model that treats memory as a rigid, linear, one-dimensional array while modern software deliberately clusters data by related regions and columns, creating a structural mismatch between hardware and data layout.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Frames the memory wall as a solvable addressing-semantics problem rather than a physics limit — a thesis that favors architectural challengers over incumbents optimizing bandwidth alone.
insights.quote: Our ultra-fast cores remain trapped in a 40-year-old architectural mindset, viewing memory as a rigid, linear, one-dimensional array.
insights.locator: Our ultra-fast cores remain trapped

insights.claim: With 128 cores each requesting narrow 64-byte cache lines scattered across the RAM footprint, cache-coherency maintenance forces millions of broadcast snoop queries that gridlock the internal interconnect fabric exactly when it should be maximizing useful data throughput.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Coherence control traffic — not DRAM bandwidth — is named as the binding constraint, redirecting attention to on-die fabric and directory design as the scarce resource in many-core scaling.
insights.quote: Cores relentlessly request narrow 64-byte cache lines scattered haphazardly across the RAM footprint.
insights.locator: When 128 cores concurrently drive modern analytical workloads

insights.claim: Flattening spatially correlated data into a one-dimensional address tape destroys structure at ingestion and then burns watts and cycles reconstructing it by brute force, turning the processor into a space heater.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Ties the memory wall directly to datacenter power draw, the metric hyperscalers are currently most constrained by — an efficiency argument, not just a speed one.
insights.quote: The processor effectively turns into a massive space heater, wasting watts and cycles trying to reconstruct, through brute force, a spatial structure it destroyed during ingestion.
insights.locator: When software needs to analyze just a single face

insights.claim: The proposed design converts physical addresses into Z-Order (Morton) layout inside the MMU/TLB itself at a deterministic cost of exactly one clock cycle, with a dedicated hardware decoder converting back to standard physical layout at the memory controller boundary, also in 1T.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: The claimed 1T fixed overhead is the whole commercial case — if real, the change is nearly free on the critical path, which is the key technical claim to stress-test before believing the rest.
insights.quote: The Z-Order format conversion is baked right into the Memory Management Unit (MMU/TLB), incurring a deterministic latency penalty of exactly one clock cycle (1T).
insights.locator: The Core Architectural Logic of Z-Order Address Space

insights.claim: The Z-Order transformation leaves the lower 6 bits of a 48-bit physical address untouched as the 64-byte cache-line offset, splits the remaining bits into equal MSB and LSB windows, and interleaves LSB bits onto even positions and MSB bits onto odd positions of the new address purely through fixed wiring.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: The mechanism is static wiring rather than logic or lookup, meaning near-zero area and power cost — the kind of change a licensable IP block could plausibly deliver.
insights.quote: Bits derived from the right-hand window (LSB) are mapped exclusively onto the even positions of the newly minted address (0, 2, 4, 6...), while bits originating from the left-hand window (MSB) are mapped onto the odd positions
insights.locator: Interleaving via Wiring

insights.claim: Under Z-Order addressing, loop-interchange optimization becomes a native hardware property, so software traversing data by row or by column sees a consistently high and stable cache hit rate regardless of loop ordering.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Would erode a large body of hand-tuned software and compiler optimization value — a risk to performance-library moats and a tailwind for naive-code workloads on such silicon.
insights.quote: Software becomes largely immune to the performance asymmetries caused by loop ordering: whether you traverse data by row or by column, the cache hit rate remains consistently high and stable.
insights.locator: Traditionally, simply reversing the way we traverse a matrix

insights.claim: The design's guiding principle is that a cache is not a storage array but a data structure etched into silicon, so software-domain techniques like geometric indices and min/max statistical data skipping should be grafted directly onto L2 and L3 hardware.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: A transferable mental model: the next wave of hardware differentiation may come from porting proven database and storage-engine tricks into cache controllers.
insights.quote: an L3 cache is ultimately nothing more than a complex collection of data structures etched directly into silicon
insights.locator: Rethinking The L3 Cache As Hardwired Data Structures

insights.claim: The proposal deliberately splits cache philosophy by tier: private L1 and L2 stay at classic 64-byte line granularity for raw local execution speed, while the shared L3 abandons lines entirely and operates on 4 KB mini-pages.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Micro/macro granularity asymmetry is the reusable design pattern here — watch for it appearing in commercial cache hierarchies as a way to cut coherence traffic without touching core pipelines.
insights.quote: At the micro level, the private L1 and L2 caches nestled adjacent to the cores continue to run unlocked at high frequencies, operating at a granular, classic 64-byte line level
insights.locator: Spatial Locality And Micro-to-Macro Cache Asymmetry

insights.claim: In a Z-Order layout a 4 KB L3 mini-page is not a linear strip of a DRAM row but a dense spatial hypercube, so each fill captures horizontal and vertical matrix neighbors simultaneously and pre-loads the elements the next algorithm iteration will need.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Explains why the design claims outsized gains on matrix and columnar workloads specifically — the benefit is workload-shaped, so any real product would be a niche accelerator, not a broad server CPU.
insights.quote: Within a Z-Order layout, such a mini-page is no longer a long, linear strip of a RAM row, but rather a dense spatial hypercube.
insights.locator: Conversely, at the macro level, the massive 512 MB L3 cache

insights.claim: Doubling private L2 to 2 MB per core costs roughly +2T of access latency from SRAM array physics, but the author argues the tradeoff is worth it because 2 MB maps exactly onto the Linux kernel's 2 MB Huge Page allocation window, letting a core anchor an entire working set locally.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Concrete example of co-designing cache capacity to OS page granularity — a cheap, checkable heuristic for evaluating whether a vendor's cache sizing is arbitrary or software-aware.
insights.quote: the 2 MB L2 footprint mathematically maps directly to the 2 MB Huge Page allocation window within the Linux kernel
insights.locator: L2 Cache Scaling And The Tropf-Hertzog Engine

insights.claim: The article's own numbers are internally loose: it describes a 512 MB total L3 while also citing a 16 MB L3 slice per CCX across 16 CCXs, which multiplies to 256 MB rather than 512 MB.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: A flag on rigor: the piece is a conceptual proposal by a practitioner, not a verified microarchitecture spec, so treat its quantitative claims as illustrative rather than modelled.
insights.quote: bypassing redundant scans across the massive 16 MB L3 cache slice
insights.locator: Dual-Barrier Ingestion And Silicon-Level Power Efficiency

insights.claim: Rather than one centralized snoop filter, the design slices a 4-bit Counting Bloom Filter into 16 microscopic 32 KB segments instantiated inside each NoC router adjacent to each CCX, for a total die footprint of just 512 KB.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: 512 KB of added SRAM to eliminate the majority of broadcast snoops is an extraordinary claimed area-for-bandwidth trade — the cheapest lever in the whole proposal if it holds.
insights.quote: the global filter is sliced into 16 microscopic 32 KB segments. These are physically instantiated inside each NoC router, directly adjacent to each of the 16 Core Complex Dies (CCXs) – representing a total silicon footprint of just 512 KB across the entire die.
insights.locator: Mitigating Interconnect Noise Via Distributed NoC Bloom Filters

insights.claim: Choosing 4 bits per Bloom counter is not arbitrary: it packs exactly two indices per byte for byte-level alignment, enabling decode and lookup within a 1T to 2T window.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Illustrates that filter latency, not filter accuracy, is the binding design constraint at NoC speeds — relevant when assessing any vendor's snoop-filter claims.
insights.quote: By utilizing a granularity of 4 bits per counter, the structure aligns perfectly at the byte level (packing two indices per byte), enabling decoding and lookup operations within a tight 1T to 2T window.
insights.locator: Mapping this framework onto an AMD Turin-class topography

insights.claim: The distributed Bloom filter converts coherence from broadcast to routed delivery, steering the vast majority of cache-coherency traffic via direct point-to-point routes to the specific CCX that actually holds the requested data.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Broadcast-to-unicast conversion is the single highest-leverage change for many-core scaling; it is the mechanism to look for in any next-generation server interconnect roadmap.
insights.quote: it drastically eliminates redundant snoops, steering the vast majority of cache-coherency traffic via direct Point-to-Point routes straight to the specific CCX that actually holds the requested data
insights.locator: This global filter tracks active pages at a macro level

insights.claim: The admitted fatal flaw of Z-Order and other space-filling curves is that quadrant jumps create massive linear address gaps, so a conventional binary search over a geometric bounding box fails outright because valid and invalid data domains interleave chaotically.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: The author naming the weakness of his own core idea is the credibility hinge — and the gap problem is why prior Morton-order hardware attempts have not shipped.
insights.quote: The fatal flaw of space-filling curves like the Z-Order layout is that they generate massive linear gaps when jumping from one quadrant to another.
insights.locator: The fatal flaw of space-filling curves

insights.claim: The gap problem is solved in hardware using BIGMIN and LITMAX functions from the 1981 Tropf-Hertzog algorithm published in Multidimensional Range Search in Dynamically Balanced Trees, letting the L2 compute the end of the valid block and the start of the next useful sequence on the fly and forward-leap over invalid address intervals.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: A 45-year-old database indexing algorithm being proposed as silicon logic shows how much unexploited prior art sits between the DB and hardware communities — a source of defensible patents.
insights.quote: leveraging the 1981 Tropf-Hertzog algorithm from the paper Multidimensional Range Search in Dynamically Balanced Trees, published by Vieweg Verlag in Wiesbaden, Germany
insights.locator: To safeguard this expanded 2MB space

insights.claim: Eight boundary-level Min/Max range filters at L2 are claimed to return a mathematically sound negative answer in 95 percent of cases within a 1T latency window, deflecting requests before the 2 MB tag array is searched.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: The 95 percent figure is the load-bearing performance assumption and is asserted without simulation data — the number to demand evidence for before valuing the concept.
insights.quote: the range filters and Tropf-Hertzog optimizations deliver a mathematically sound "NO" in 95 percent of cases within a tight 1T latency window
insights.locator: Driven by this mathematical logic

insights.claim: A second set of 8 Tropf-Hertzog Min/Max filters is duplicated at the L3 boundary specifically to catch probabilistic false positives leaking out of the NoC Bloom filters, triggering a Fast Reject in 1T before any L3 slice scan occurs.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: The dual-barrier pattern acknowledges that probabilistic filters need a deterministic backstop — a design requirement any competing snoop-filter implementation must also satisfy.
insights.quote: if a junk request evades the network-level filtering, the 8 geometric filters inside the L3 trigger a Fast Reject within a tight 1T window
insights.locator: Dual-Barrier Ingestion And Silicon-Level Power Efficiency

insights.claim: In conventional microarchitectures an immense amount of energy is burned powering up megabytes of SRAM tag arrays during speculative lookups for data that may not even be resident in cache.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Identifies an overlooked power sink inside CPUs that is invisible in TDP marketing but directly affects rack density economics.
insights.quote: an immense amount of energy is wasted by continuously powering up megabytes of SRAM Tag arrays during speculative lookups
insights.locator: In conventional microarchitectures

insights.claim: The double shield of Counting Bloom filters plus Tropf-Hertzog min/max logic at each cache island's ingress allows high-density SRAM arrays to remain in a low-power state for the vast majority of transactions and to wake only when a hit is certain.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Reframes filtering as a power technology rather than a latency technology — the more investable framing given that datacenter buildouts are power-constrained.
insights.quote: They are awakened and dynamically powered up only when a cache hit is an absolute certainty.
insights.locator: Under this new paradigm, thanks to the double shield

insights.claim: Suppressing redundant control traffic across the on-die NoC fabric is presented as a direct lever on electrical power consumption, not merely on throughput.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Supports a view that interconnect efficiency gains show up in rack-level power budgets, which is where hyperscaler procurement decisions are increasingly made.
insights.quote: Eliminating redundant control traffic across the internal Network-on-Chip (NoC) fabric drastically slashes electrical power consumption.
insights.locator: Silicon Power Conservation

insights.claim: SmartNICs pushing network traffic into system RAM via RDMA extract a severe hidden tax because the NIC must constantly query the CPU's cache state, and this barrage of parasitic snoop requests stalls core execution paths precisely during heavy Big Data and AI workloads.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Names a cost of RDMA and DPU offload that vendors rarely quantify — relevant to assessing whether DPU attach rates actually deliver the promised host-CPU savings.
insights.quote: This uninterrupted barrage of parasitic snoop requests forces the CPU cores to stall their execution paths for fractions of a second, triggering cascading pipeline bottlenecks
insights.locator: SmartNIC/DPU Offloading and the Tropf-Hertzog Geometric Shield

insights.claim: Giving the SmartNIC direct access to a boundary-level Tropf-Hertzog 'Geometric Shield' lets it resolve coherence questions in a 1T window without waking the processor, claimed to yield 0 percent pipeline stalls from network-coherency management.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: If I/O coherence can be answered at the cache boundary rather than by the cores, the host-CPU tax of high-rate networking collapses — a structural argument for tighter NIC-cache co-design.
insights.quote: The CPU cores remain completely unburdened, experiencing 0% pipeline stalls and continuing to run at maximum frequency without wasting precious clock cycles on network-coherency management.
insights.locator: Zero Core Interruptions

insights.claim: Real-world network bandwidth is argued to be limited today not by the wire but by the queue latencies of an overloaded CPU, so removing the coherence bottleneck lets SmartNIC throughput saturate.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Suggests that deployed NIC line rates are under-utilized for host-side reasons — a check on revenue assumptions tied to ever-faster NIC SKUs.
insights.quote: Real-world network bandwidth scales dramatically because the SmartNIC is no longer bottlenecked by the queue latencies of an overloaded CPU.
insights.locator: Throughput Saturation

insights.claim: 4 KB macro-granularity transfers amortize inter-socket bus latency by paying the penalty once to ingest a dense spatial hypercube of coordinates and neighbors that will be consumed immediately, instead of repeatedly paying it for scattered lines.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Large-granularity transfer as a latency-amortization strategy applies equally to multi-socket, chiplet and rack-scale fabrics — a general rule for evaluating disaggregation designs.
insights.quote: The system pays the bus latency penalty exactly once to ingest a massive payload of coordinates and neighboring data points that will be consumed immediately.
insights.locator: Scaling Out: Inter-Socket Mechanics And CXL Traffic Saving

insights.claim: Local filters acting as a structural isolator drop junk requests on the die before they cross the motherboard, preserving inter-processor bus bandwidth exclusively for actual data payloads.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Filtering at the source rather than the destination is the scaling principle; it determines whether multi-socket systems degrade gracefully as core counts rise.
insights.quote: Inter-processor buses remain clear of junk traffic, preserving their entire bandwidth strictly for actual data payloads.
insights.locator: Simultaneously, the symbiosis between the 16 CCXs

insights.claim: The author asserts the future of the datacenter belongs to disaggregated architectures where RAM pools live in separate racks accessed over CXL, but flags fabric-cabling wire latency as CXL's own steep tax.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Memory disaggregation is treated as inevitable but latency-gated, meaning value accrues to whoever solves the tail-latency problem rather than to the protocol itself.
insights.quote: the future of the datacenter belongs to disaggregated architectures, where massive pools of RAM are decoupled into separate racks and accessed via the Compute Express Link (CXL) protocol
insights.locator: Looking further ahead, beyond the limits of the motherboard

insights.claim: Extending the global Counting Bloom filter to track CXL-mapped address spaces turns it into a CXL Traffic Saver that aborts a request at the silicon boundary on a predicted miss, claimed to recapture roughly 250 nanoseconds of parasitic tail latency per avoided traversal plus wattage.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Puts a hard number on the cost of a wasted CXL round trip — the metric by which CXL memory-pooling products should be judged, since miss handling dominates pooled-memory economics.
insights.quote: This mechanism instantly recaptures roughly 250 nanoseconds of parasitic tail-latency and saves significant wattage, ensuring that transactions only leave the chip via CXL when there is near-absolute probabilistic certainty of a hit.
insights.locator: The request is terminated on the spot

insights.claim: When a CXL traversal is unavoidable, it should retrieve a full 4 KB mini-page in Z-Order layout so the physical distance penalty is paid once for a complete hypercube of analytical data.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Implies pooled CXL memory will favor page-granular, layout-aware access patterns over cache-line semantics, which shapes which workloads can actually use disaggregated memory.
insights.locator: When a CXL traversal does occur

insights.claim: The author explicitly scopes the design as a specialized processor, not a general-purpose CPU, naming seismic and oil and gas exploration, AI/ML, distributed SQL analytical engines, scientific computing, engineering simulation, aerospace, defense and space as target sectors.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Self-limiting TAM: this is a domain-specific-architecture play competing with GPUs and accelerators, not a challenge to x86 or Arm server volume.
insights.quote: These innovations are not engineered for a traditional, general-purpose processor forced to execute arbitrary workloads.
insights.locator: These innovations are not engineered

insights.claim: AMD's 'Turin' Epyc 9005 with 128 cores across 16 CCX modules is used only as a structural reference topology for a theoretical analysis, meaning nothing in the piece reflects an actual AMD roadmap or implementation.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Guards against misreading this as AMD product intelligence — the Epyc reference is a modelling substrate, not a signal about future AMD silicon.
insights.quote: I adopted the topology of a cutting-edge server processor as our baseline model and structural framework: the AMD "Turin" Epyc 9005 architecture, featuring 128 high-performance compute cores symmetrically distributed across 16 Core Complex (CCX) modules.
insights.locator: The Architectural Paradigm Shift

insights.claim: The design migrates decades of manual software bit-twiddling for spatial locality into hardwired processor logic, effectively arguing that work currently done in application code is misplaced and should be a hardware service.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: A hardware-absorbs-software thesis: where it holds, specialist optimization vendors lose pricing power and silicon vendors gain it.
insights.quote: For decades, software engineers have spent immense effort executing complex bit-twiddling techniques to manually simulate spatial locality within their codebases.
insights.locator: Mission Accomplished: Smashing The Memory Wall

insights.claim: The piece is authored by a senior technical business analyst at Integrated Data Systems SRL in Bucharest with a decade of prior software and technical lead roles at Citibank Romania, published as a reader-submitted soapbox rather than as vendor or analyst research.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: Provenance caps the weight of the claims: a practitioner's design thesis with no simulation, silicon or vendor backing should be filed as an idea to track, not as evidence of a product cycle.
insights.quote: Vasile spent a decade on various software and technical lead positions at Citibank Romania and is now a senior technical business analyst at Integrated Data Systems SRL, a consulting organization based on Bucharest.
insights.locator: Cristian Vasile is a long-time reader

insights.claim: The L3 ingesting from RAM in 4 KB blocks is deliberately aligned to both native Linux OS pages and the block boundaries of NVMe flash and SSD storage, extending the alignment argument from CPU to the storage path.
insights.speaker: Cristian Vasile
insights.so_what: End-to-end 4 KB alignment from SSD block to L3 line is the kind of full-stack coherence that makes columnar analytics pipelines faster without code changes — a checklist item for evaluating analytics appliances.
insights.quote: the global L3 cache ingests data from system RAM in large 4 KB blocks, providing strict alignment with native Linux operating system pages and the block boundaries of high-speed NVMe flash and SSD storage infrastructures
insights.locator: Dual-Barrier Ingestion And Silicon-Level Power Efficiency
